title: A Visitor for the Choir
premise: Gideon Pemberton returns to the drowned village of Hollowmere to bury their twin sister Wren, only to find the body in the coffin is not Wren's—and that Wren may never have left. When an excavation crew for the new reservoir breaches a door sealed from the inside beneath the old chapel, Gideon learns the village choir has been singing a lullaby to something buried there for two hundred years, and with the singers dead or scattered, the song has gone unfinished. As the harvest moon approaches, the thing below begins finishing the verse itself, wearing the voices of the missing, and Gideon must decide whether love means freeing what their family helped bury or keeping it starved forever. In the end, Gideon sings the last verse alone—changing one word—and seals the door from the inside with Wren's help, trading their own voice for the town's survival.
about_author: Orsen Voss is the pen name of a former church organist who spent a decade cataloguing hymnals in rural parish archives before turning to fiction. They write horror about small communities, inherited guilt, and the songs people sing to keep things asleep.

chapters.title: The Wrong Body
chapters.summary: Gideon arrives in Hollowmere for Wren's funeral and insists on viewing the body, finding a stranger's face in the coffin. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: grief curdling into dread as the funeral director's practiced evasions reveal the whole town knew.

chapters.title: A Town That Won't Look at You
chapters.summary: Gideon stays to investigate, canvassing neighbors who answer doors but not questions. Old Mrs. Halloway slips them a hymnal page torn from a choir book. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: isolation sharpening into resolve; the found-family thread begins with Halloway's wary kindness.

chapters.title: What the Excavation Found
chapters.summary: The reservoir crew breaches a stone door beneath the chapel foundation—scratched smooth on the inside. Foreman Daley shows Gideon photographs before the company confiscates them. POV: Daley. Emotional beat: professional pride collapsing into superstitious fear.

chapters.title: Voices in the Water Table
chapters.summary: Night noises begin: singing under the floorboards, in the well, in the drainpipes—Wren's voice among them. Gideon records it and hears harmonies no single throat could make. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: hope weaponized; longing for the twin makes the haunting seductive.

chapters.title: Halloway's Confession
chapters.summary: Mrs. Halloway reveals she sang alto in the Hollowmere Choir until 1998, when they stopped mid-verse and three members vanished. The song isn't worship—it's containment. POV: Halloway. Emotional beat: guilt of the complicit; duty versus mercy established as the book's central fault line.

chapters.title: The Verse That Was Never Written
chapters.summary: Gideon studies the hymnal: the song has four written verses and a fifth that exists only in the singers' memories, passed orally, deliberately unrecorded. Whoever finishes it decides what wakes. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: intellectual horror—the realization that knowledge itself is the trap.

chapters.title: Daley's Crew Stops Coming to Work
chapters.summary: Two workers go missing after night shifts near the breach. The third, Petey Oakes, is found on his porch, humming, unable to stop. POV: Petey. Emotional beat: body horror of possession; the corruption of power as the thing below borrows voices.

chapters.title: Wren's Room, Unchanged
chapters.summary: Gideon breaks into the shuttered family house and finds Wren's room preserved, dust undisturbed for three years—except fresh flowers on the sill, cut this week. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: the past refusing to stay buried; love against duty turns inward.

chapters.title: The Company Man
chapters.summary: A reservoir executive, Corliss, arrives to spin the disappearances and quietly asks Gideon what they know about 'the Pemberton obligation.' Their grandfather signed something in 1946. POV: Corliss. Emotional beat: institutional evil; power corrupting through paperwork and denial.

chapters.title: Séance of the Surviving Choir
chapters.summary: Gideon gathers the last living choir members—Halloway, deaf tenor Amos Pike, and defected soprano Ruth Ellery—who haven't spoken in twenty-five years. Together they reconstruct why they stopped singing. POV: Ruth. Emotional beat: found family reassembling around shared trauma.

chapters.title: What Grandfather Buried
chapters.summary: In the chapel archive, Gideon finds the 1946 agreement: the Pembertons were hereditary 'first voices,' obligated to lead the final verse when the seal weakened. Their signature line reads 'and my issue after me.' POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: inheritance as sentence; rage at ancestors.

chapters.title: It Learns Our Names
chapters.summary: The thing below begins speaking through townsfolk in daylight now—first mimicry, then persuasion, offering each person their deepest want. It offers Gideon Wren, alive. POV: multiple brief vignettes. Emotional beat: temptation distributed; the town fracturing along private desires.

chapters.title: Ruth Sings Along
chapters.summary: Ruth, grieving her dead son, accepts the offer and sings the fifth verse's opening line at the breach. The door groans; the reservoir water turns black. She vanishes smiling. POV: Ruth. Emotional beat: tragic surrender—the cost of love without limits.

chapters.title: Amos Who Cannot Hear It
chapters.summary: Deaf Amos becomes the only clear-headed adult in town—he can't be tempted by a voice he can't hear. He teaches Gideon the verse in hand-signs, felt through the piano's soundboard. POV: Amos. Emotional beat: tenderness and ingenuity; disability as unexpected armor.

chapters.title: Corliss Seals the Road
chapters.summary: The company locks down Hollowmere, cutting phones, framing the disappearances as a chemical leak. Corliss plans to flood the site early—with the town's remaining residents as ballast. POV: Corliss. Emotional beat: banal evil reaching its logical end; stakes become communal.

chapters.title: Wren, Finally
chapters.summary: Wren appears to Gideon at the waterline—not a ghost exactly, but a half-finished echo the thing uses as bait, except parts of her are genuinely still her. She begs Gideon to finish the song and free her. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: the cruelest choice made flesh; love against duty at full pressure.

chapters.title: The Harvest Moon Rises
chapters.summary: Moonrise. The breach opens fully. The thing rises wearing a chorus of stolen faces—Petey, Ruth, the missing crew—and begins singing the fifth verse in every voice in town at once. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: apocalyptic set piece; beauty and horror fused.

chapters.title: First Voice
chapters.summary: Gideon takes the hereditary position at the breach and begins the counter-verse, Amos signing the melody, Halloway holding the harmony. The duel of songs tears at Gideon's memory of Wren, which the thing weaponizes note by note. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: climax of will; singing as sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Changed Word
chapters.summary: At the verse's final line, instead of the binding word ('stay'), Gideon sings 'rest'—freeing the trapped souls, including Wren's echo, while letting the ancient hunger dissolve rather than sleep. The stolen voices release all at once. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: catharsis; love fulfilled by letting go.

chapters.title: The Price of the Last Note
chapters.summary: Gideon wakes mute—their voice left behind in the closing dark. Wren's echo, freed, presses one hand to their chest in farewell before going out like a candle. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: grief transfigured; the cost paid without regret.

chapters.title: After the Flood
chapters.summary: The reservoir fills over the sealed chapel. Corliss is disgraced when Petey's testimony surfaces; the survivors—Gideon, Amos, Halloway—form an odd household above the waterline. POV: Halloway. Emotional beat: quiet aftermath; found family solidified in shared silence.

chapters.title: Coda: A Visitor for the Choir
chapters.summary: Months later, Gideon, voiceless, conducts a rebuilt Hollowmere choir by hand, teaching children a song with only four verses. On the last page of the new hymnal, someone has penciled a fifth—unsigned. Gideon smiles and closes the book. POV: Gideon. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution; some songs keep themselves.
